topic: How to Pick Colors That Don't Look AI-Generated — accent discipline, why indigo/blue defaults scream slop, picking one accent and committing, warm vs cold neutrals
title: Why every AI app is the same shade of blue
caption:
Ever notice how every new AI app ships the same indigo? That's not a coincidence — it's the default.

Bootstrap blue, Tailwind indigo, #6366F1 everywhere. Reaching for blue is the fastest way to look generic.

The fix:
01. Pick ONE accent and commit — use it for actions, not decoration
02. Kill the default indigo/blue
03. Nudge your neutrals warm or cool (pure grey looks cheap)
04. Check your palette in greyscale first

Color is a choice. Make one.

topic: The Spacing Rules That Make UI Look Designed — the 8pt grid, generous section padding, grouping by proximity, why cramped UI reads as amateur
title: Same layout, way more space — that's the whole trick
caption:
Most UI that feels a little 'off' has the same problem: no space.

Good news is you don't have to redesign anything. Usually the fix is just room. Put everything on an 8pt grid so your gaps stop looking random. Give your sections way more padding than feels necessary. Keep related stuff close together, and push the unrelated stuff apart.

Same layout, more breathing room, and suddenly it looks like someone who knew what they were doing built it.

topic: Dark Mode Mistakes That Make Your App Look Cheap — pure black vs warm charcoal, dimming text instead of pure white, desaturating accents on dark, elevation through lightness
title: Your dark mode looks cheap, and it's an easy fix
caption:
Dark mode is more than a black background and white text. That's usually why it ends up looking cheap.

A few quick fixes. Skip pure black — it's harsh and makes every edge buzz. Use a warm charcoal instead, around #1C1A17. Don't use pure white text either; pull it back to a soft cream so it doesn't glare. Take that bright accent from light mode and knock the saturation down so it glows instead of blinding people. And forget shadows — in dark mode, higher surfaces just get lighter.

Do those four things and your dark mode stops looking like a default and starts looking designed.

topic: How to Design a Hero Section That Actually Hooks — clear value prop over clever copy, one CTA, showing the product not an illustration, the fold line
title: You've got 3 seconds before they leave your hero
caption:
People decide whether to stay in about 3 seconds. Your hero section has to do a lot in that time.

Skip the clever headline and just say what your thing does, plainly. Give people one button, not five — pick the action you want most and make it obvious. Show a real screenshot of the product instead of some generic illustration, so they can see what they're getting. And put all of it above the fold, because you should assume nobody scrolls.

Clear message, one action, real product, above the fold. That's a hero that actually hooks.

topic: Pricing Page UI That Makes People Pick the Right Plan — highlighting the plan you want chosen, annual toggle defaults, anchoring, cutting plan clutter
title: Your pricing page is quietly leaving money on the table
caption:
Most pricing pages make people work too hard, and they leave without buying.

Make it easier. Highlight the plan you actually want people to pick — badge it, make it bigger, give it the accent color. Default the billing toggle to annual and show the savings right there. Put a pricey plan first so the one you want looks reasonable next to it. And cut the clutter — three plans max, not six columns of tiny checkmarks nobody reads.

Guide the choice instead of leaving people to figure it out. They'll thank you by actually converting.

topic: The Screens Everyone Forgets to Design — empty states, loading states, error states, the zero-data first-run experience
title: The screens everyone forgets to design
caption:
Everyone designs the happy path. Almost nobody designs the empty screen, the loading screen, or the error screen — and those are the ones people actually hit first.

Design the empty state: a friendly line and one clear button beats a blank void. Show a loading state so a slow screen doesn't feel broken — skeletons or a spinner, anything. Write error messages a human would understand, and tell people what to do next. And nail the first-run experience, because the zero-data moment decides if anyone sticks around.

The boring screens are where good apps pull away from sloppy ones.

topic: UI That Breaks on Mobile (And How to Fix It) — touch target sizes, sticky mobile CTAs, text that's too small, tables that don't reflow
title: Looks great on your laptop. Falls apart on a phone.
caption:
Your site looks great on your big monitor. On a phone? Probably a mess. Here's what usually breaks.

Tap targets that are too small — make every button at least 44px so people can actually hit them. Your main CTA scrolling away — pin it to the bottom so it's always a thumb-tap away. Text that's too tiny — 16px is the floor for body copy, anything less and people are pinching to zoom. And wide tables that overflow — reflow them into stacked cards so each row reads top to bottom.

Design for the thumb first and mobile stops being an afterthought.
